t:
(a) 
The first paragraph under the heading “Hospital Corps,” page 572, volume 39, of the Statutes at Large (Act of August 29, 1916), as amended by the Act of April 18, 1946 (Public Law 347, Seventy-ninth Congress, second session), is hereby further amended to read as follows:
 “Hereafter the authorized strength of the Hospital Corps of the Navy shall equal 3½ per centum of the authorized enlisted strength of the Navy and Marine Corps. The Secretary of the Navy is authorized, in his discretion, to establish such grades and ratings in the Hospital Corps as he may deem necessary in the proper administration of such corps: 
Provided, That enlisted men of other ratings in the Navy and in the Marine Corps shall be eligible for transfer to the Hospital Corps, and men of that corps to other ratings in the Navy and the Marine Corps.”



 
    (b) The second paragraph under such heading is hereby amended to read as follows:
 “The Secretary of the Navy may hereafter appoint as many warrant officers in the Hospital Corps, as may be deemed necessary, from the rating of chief petty officer or petty officer, first class, in the Hospital Corps: 
Provided, That no person shall be appointed pursuant hereto until he shall have established his mental, moral, physical, and professional qualifications to the satisfaction of the Secretary of the Navy:


Provided further, That the warrant officers now in the Hospital Corps of the United States Navy or hereafter appointed therein in accordance with the provisions of this Act shall have the same rank, pay, and allowances as are now or may hereafter be allowed other warrant officers.”

fable.w: The section sets the authorized strength of the Navy Hospital Corps and lets the Secretary of the Navy establish grades and appoint warrant officers at his own discretion. The tempting reading is that the Secretary's authority to "establish" grades is a grant of rulemaking power, but the text does not call for regulations, comment, hearings, or consultation with anyone outside the federal government. Every actor involved (the Secretary, enlisted men, warrant officers) is inside the federal government, so this is internal personnel administration, not participation.
fable.s: The Secretary of the Navy is authorized, in his discretion, to establish such grades and ratings in the Hospital Corps as he may deem necessary in the proper administration of such corps

qwen_block.w: This section grants the Secretary of the Navy authority to manage internal personnel structures (grades, ratings, appointments) within the Navy and Marine Corps. All actors involved (the Secretary, enlisted men, warrant officers) are federal employees or officials. There is no requirement to consult with or coordinate with any outside parties (states, public, experts, etc.) before making these decisions.
qwen_block.s: The Secretary of the Navy is authorized, in his discretion, to establish such grades and ratings in the Hospital Corps as he may deem necessary in the proper administration of such corps

opus.w: This section sets the strength, grades and warrant-officer appointments of the Navy Hospital Corps. Everyone involved (the Secretary of the Navy and Navy and Marine Corps personnel) is inside the federal government. The Secretary's discretion to set grades is internal administrative authority, not a grant of rulemaking power and not consultation with outside parties, so it is not participation.
opus.s: The Secretary of the Navy is authorized, in his discretion, to establish such grades and ratings in the Hospital Corps as he may deem necessary in the proper administration of such corps
opus.b: Step 1, the tempting reading: the Secretary of the Navy is given discretion to "establish such grades and ratings" and to appoint warrant officers, which might look like rulemaking authority (as in Example 6). That reading fails. The section never mentions regulations or rulemaking. It only grants internal personnel and administrative discretion, and every actor is inside the federal government: the Secretary, Navy enlisted men and warrant officers. No outside party is consulted or involved.

qwen_chat.w: The Secretary of the Navy is a federal official, and the people being appointed are members of the military (federal employees). There is no involvement of outside parties in the decision-making process. It looks like participation because it involves the Secretary of the Navy making decisions about appointments and qualifications.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of the Navy is authorized, in his discretion, to establish such grades and ratings in the Hospital Corps as he may deem necessary in the proper administration of such corps
